name: Activa radium cosmetics

card.summary: A French early-20th-century cosmetic brand, Crème Activa, that marketed radium's science prestige for beauty.
card.note: Historical; radium cosmetics are no longer sold. Little is documented about Activa itself.

quick.overview:
Crème Activa was a French beauty brand of the early radium craze, which promoted radium's discovery as a conquest of science for beauty. Radium-linked cosmetics promised to reduce wrinkles and make skin look younger.

Little is recorded about Activa's formula or sales; it is best understood within the wider radium cosmetics trade.
quick.how: Radium cosmetics were creams and similar products applied to skin; brands sold them as anti-aging and complexion products.
quick.risks: Radium's dangers became widely known through the Radium Girls and 1931 death of Eben Byers; the 1938 US law tightened cosmetic claims and safety.

lead: Activa is named among brands that began exploiting radium's prestige in the 1910s; Crème Activa advertised radium's discovery as 'a wonderful conquest of science in the service of beauty'.[1]

Radium cosmetics in general promised to fight wrinkles, unwanted hair and crow's feet, and some suggested 'face lifting without plastic surgery'.[1] Radium was often advertised in products that had no real link to it.[1]
Details of Activa's composition and history are not documented in accessible sources.

angle.text: Brands claimed radium creams rejuvenated skin; no such result is documented.

paras: Radium was isolated in 1898 and the boom ran through the 1920s and 1930s.[1] The AMA withdrew approval of radium for internal use in 1933 and the 1938 Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act required ingredient labeling and limited false claims.[1] Tho-Radia, a French line, was sold from 1932 to 1968 and contained radium and thorium early on.[2]

timeline.event: US cosmetic law requires safety proof and limits false claims.[1]
